extracted.intended_audience: journalists and media professionals who report on crime and crime victims
extracted.subtask_description: A practical, trauma-informed guidance set for journalists covering crime victims across breaking news, feature, and high-impact enterprise reporting—covering interviewing, logistics, privacy, multimedia, ethics, working with service providers, and reporter self-care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the media's impact
rubrics_metrics.description: News media have enormous impact on victims, criminal and juvenile justice systems, and public policy; journalists should understand and responsibly shape public understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide accurate, fair, balanced, and complete coverage; explain how justice systems work while respecting victims' needs and rights so the public can make informed choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt reporting to Act I/II/III
rubrics_metrics.description: Different types of crime coverage—Act I (breaking news), Act II (feature stories), Act III (high-impact/enterprise stories)—pose different challenges and require tailored approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For breaking news, move quickly but sensitively; for features, allow time to capture feelings and context; for high-impact stories, plan extensively and prepare for multiple/lengthy interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize distractions when approaching victims
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach victims without visible equipment to make a human connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever possible, approach victims without notebooks, recorders, cameras, or lights; if they agree, then request permission to use equipment; small steps give victims a sense of control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify yourself clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediately tell the person you are a reporter and your news organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trauma can impair comprehension; clear identification ensures the person understands they are speaking to media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge the victim's experience with empathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Use compassionate, appropriate phrases to open contact with victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'safe' phrases such as 'I am sorry for what happened to you' or 'I am sorry for your loss' to establish human connection and avoid inadvertent offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give victims a clear reason to speak
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the purpose and importance of the story to encourage participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Your information may help with the investigation,' 'Members of the community want to know how you are doing,' 'We want to verify what others have said.' Avoid vague or coercive language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the victim how much time you need
rubrics_metrics.description: State clearly that you only need a few minutes (or X minutes) to respect immediate priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explaining a short time commitment increases the likelihood of securing an interview when victims have pressing needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect refusals; take no for an answer
rubrics_metrics.description: If victims decline, treat them courteously and avoid pressuring them to talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that a story may still run and that this is an opportunity to tell their side, but do not imply coercion or use threatening tones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave contact information and follow-up options
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer a business card or a note explaining the story mission and how to contact you later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When people are not home or decline initially, leaving a brief compassionate note with contact information can allow them to reach out when ready.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask for alternative spokespersons
rubrics_metrics.description: When the victim declines, request names of family, friends, clergy, or official representatives who might speak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid defaulting to neighbors or coworkers who may not know the victim's situation well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put victims at physical ease
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange comfortable logistics for interviews—offer a chair, avoid intrusive lighting, and be mindful of touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small gestures (chair, water, tissues) help victims feel safe; in broadcast, hand lavalier microphones to the subject rather than touching them; bright lights may be intrusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask permission to record
rubrics_metrics.description: Request consent before recording audio or video to give the victim control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit consent both respects the person and reduces misunderstandings; offer to turn recorders/cameras off for sensitive material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Come prepared with basic comforts
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring supplies such as water, tissues, and items to freshen the subject before recording/photography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Victims may appreciate (and later tell others about) small comforts like a damp tissue or comb prior to being photographed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish ground rules about confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify 'off the record' conventions and give victims the power to stop recording or video.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain any limits to confidentiality and ensure victims understand how their words may be used; allow them to turn off recorders for off-the-record information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize trauma's effects on perception and memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for how trauma can distort perceptions of time, sequence, and sensory detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify timings with external anchors (clocks, radio/TV dialogue), ask for reference points, and be cautious about treating precise time estimates as definitive—this is important for later testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid leading questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not prompt victims toward specific answers or facts they did not report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open-ended questions elicit more reliable accounts and avoid contaminating victims' recollections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid questions that imply blame
rubrics_metrics.description: Never suggest victims are at fault for their victimization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake remorse for confession; avoid phrasing that reinforces self-blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame safety guidance as risk-reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: When offering safety tips, emphasize risk-reduction strategies rather than implying victims can fully prevent victimization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid wording like 'how to avoid being a victim'; recognize there are no fail-safe prevention methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid loaded words and formulaic prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from blunt 'How do you feel?' or pressuring terms like 'closure'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recast emotional prompts empathetically ('Would you be willing to share with me... the thoughts and feelings you are experiencing?'); avoid 'closure' which can pressure victims into appearing 'okay.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask whether the person prefers 'victim' or 'survivor'
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect individual identity preferences when labeling people affected by crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some find 'survivor' empowering; others prefer 'victim'—ask to avoid inadvertent offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'alleged' carefully (apply to perpetrators, not victims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reserve 'alleged' for accused perpetrators; avoid applying it to victims as it can imply they are lying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to the person who reported the incident or use neutral language rather than implying doubt about victims' accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sensitivity when questioning about domestic violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand complex reasons victims remain with abusers (fear, children, poverty, danger in leaving).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid shaming language; demonstrate understanding of safety risks and the danger associated with leaving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for and communicate about multimedia coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Victims should be warned that coverage may include print, video, and online elements and can be widely distributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how photos and video will be used; consider additional consent steps for multimedia elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that local stories can become national
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must assume stories may reach a far broader audience than local outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handle identifying information and privacy accordingly, since online and broadcast distribution can magnify exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure training for print reporters producing video
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters who add multimedia skills need training on victim issues and visual ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ad-hoc video production by reporters without victim-sensitive training; coordinate with experienced videographers when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inform and guide citizen journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizen reporters and contributors should receive guidance on victim issues and ethical considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide resources or links for best practices; consider moderating or advising user-generated content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat online mistakes as long-lasting
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors in online coverage can persist indefinitely; exercise extra care with accuracy and privacy online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct promptly and transparently, but recognize that initial mistakes may be archived and shared widely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include victim input when managing citizen comments
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations should consider victim perspectives when deciding how to handle public comments on stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moderate comments to prevent victim harassment; involve victim services/input in policy where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographers and videographers’ special responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual journalists must exercise heightened care about intrusive images and respecting dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gratuitous images of injury or distress, respect privacy, and follow guidance to minimize re-victimization via visuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors must be aware of victim sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial decisions (headlines, photo selection, placement) can introduce problems for victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should apply victim-sensitive policies and review visuals and headlines for potential harm before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pack journalism pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist herd dynamics that increase pressure on victims and produce redundant or sensational coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate internally to reduce repeated intrusion; avoid chasing the same traumatized sources for multiple outlets without consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance news values against victim priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworthiness should not trump victims' rights and dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When news values conflict with victim needs, seek alternatives that preserve dignity (e.g., anonymize, delay publication, use alternatives to intrusive visuals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve cultural competency
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should strive to understand cultural differences and contexts affecting victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in training and consultation to avoid cultural insensitivities and to report accurately across diverse communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider pre-publication sharing cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Think carefully before sharing victim stories with subjects prior to publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the benefits of accuracy and trauma-informed practice against potential harm such as re-traumatization or coercion; do not allow pre-publication review to become editorial control by sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making the story solely about the perpetrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure victim perspectives and impacts are represented rather than focusing only on perpetrators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include victims' voices, community impact, systemic context, and restorative angles when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop accountability mechanisms for reporters and editors
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations should have ways to hold staff accountable for ethical lapses in victim reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create complaint processes, internal review, training refreshers, and advisory panels to monitor victim-sensitive coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidelines for requesting feature stories
rubrics_metrics.description: When pursuing feature or profile stories, approach subjects with time, transparency, and sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain story purpose, timeline, length, and how material will be used; be especially cautious with anniversary or continuing mystery stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts can contextualize crime and victimization but should not replace victims' voices or be used uncritically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify reliable experts, verify credentials, and avoid overreliance on punditry; make clear experts’ scope and potential biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'poster child' problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reduce victims to symbolic examples that oversimplify or exploit their experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect individuality and complexity; avoid using a single person to represent entire issues without consent and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freelancer and nonstaff accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Freelancers and stringers must adhere to the same ethical standards as staff reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure freelancers are briefed on policies, provide training/resources, and hold them to organization standards in contracts and editorial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work collaboratively with victim advocates and service providers
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordinate with advocates to facilitate sensitive, respectful coverage and help victims navigate media interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand advocates' roles, ask how they can assist, and consider joint training, advisory panels, and referral processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Provider and Media Advisory Panels
rubrics_metrics.description: Form advisory groups with victim-service providers to guide newsroom policy and practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advisory panels can advise on cultural competency, privacy, and appropriate outreach strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer newsroom tours and outreach
rubrics_metrics.description: Invite victim service providers and community stakeholders to see newsroom operations and build trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tours can demystify news production and foster cooperative relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create written ethics policies on victim coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations should formalize policies regarding interviews, images, privacy, and consent of victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should be accessible, regularly reviewed, and include training, procedures for photo/video use, and guidance on identifying sensitive cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect victims' right to privacy (intrusion, private facts, false light)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid unlawful or unethical invasions of privacy, publication of intimate private facts, or portraying victims in a misleading or damaging manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about photographing or publishing details that are not newsworthy and that could cause substantial distress; consult legal guidance and newsroom policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise caution with cameras in courtrooms
rubrics_metrics.description: Weigh the legal, ethical, and victim-protection implications of courtroom cameras and photography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow jurisdictional rules and consider the potential impact on victims, jurors, and judicial fairness before advocating for or using courtroom visuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement self-care practices for journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters covering trauma should take steps to manage vicarious trauma and stress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend time processing thoughts/feelings, take mini-breaks, derive confidence from skills, learn about trauma, turn to supportive peers/family, pursue spiritual/creative outlets, take care of the body, and seek help sooner rather than later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and explain legal/technical terminology accurately
rubrics_metrics.description: When using terms like indictment, plea agreement, restitution, victim impact statement, etc., define and apply them correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mischaracterizing legal status; explain legal procedures and terms in accessible language and be careful not to imply guilt or innocence improperly.
